Subject: Re: Follow-up from today's discovery — embeddings + migration

Great questions, Joe — glad we could connect. High level answers and a proposed next step (technical deep-dive):

High-level guidance:
- Dimensions: many customers start with 1024 or 1536 depending on model choice. 1536 (your current setting) is fine for quality; 1024 can reduce storage/latency/cost with modest quality drop for typical semantic search. We can validate with a small eval set.
- Normalization: we recommend unit-normalizing vectors for cosine at index-time (store normalized vectors) — this simplifies scoring and lets you use L2 on normalized vectors as an efficient proxy.
- Batching: for bulk ingest we typically recommend batching 512–1024 vectors per request when using our SDK with concurrency of 4–8 workers, then tune based on GPU memory/throughput.
- Migration: suggested staged approach — export existing embeddings, sample and run A/B quality tests (old vs re-embedded), then dual-write for a period before cutover. If you need to preserve 3rd-party embeddings, you can store them alongside Redwood embeddings and use a hybrid rerank.

Attachments: I've attached our migration playbook (redwood_embeddings_migration_playbook.pdf) and included a Drive link with migration checklist.

Next step proposal:
- Technical deep-dive (60m) to cover SDK setup, auth options (API key vs mTLS for Private), routing for rerankers, and a short eval run. Proposed times: Thu May 14 10am PT or Thu May 14 2pm PT.

Action: can you confirm a slot and whether your SRE will join? Also let us know which metric you'd like us to optimize for first (latency vs cost vs top-k accuracy).

Subject: Re: Follow-up from today's discovery — embeddings + migration (technical notes)

Hi Joe — quick technical notes to help your team plan. TL;DR: keep gold vectors for tail cases, unit-normalize at index-time, use progressive dual-write and validate with offline evals. Details below.

Vector dimension
- If you must preserve tail recall, a hybrid approach works well: re-embed most corpus at 1024 for cost/speed, but keep a small subset of 1536 "golden" vectors for items known to be sensitive (rare SKUs). At query time, expand candidate set to include both indexes (faster 1024 ANN + fallback to 1536 subset).

Normalization & scoring
- Store unit-normalized vectors in the index. Cosine similarity between vectors is equivalent to dot product on L2-normalized vectors; storing normalized vectors lets you use L2-based ANN libraries efficiently.
- Avoid normalizing at query-time where possible; do it once at ingest to reduce compute. Keep original unnormalized vector if you need to run cross-encoder rerankers that expect raw embeddings.

Batching & throughput
- SDK recommendations: use Redwood SDK embeddings.batch with payloads of 512–1024 vectors. For your current 16 workers of 256, you can aggregate client-side to fewer concurrent requests (e.g., 8 workers x 512) to reduce per-request overhead and be friendly to rate limits.
- For Dedicated: we expose throughput guidance per GPU pool; we can provision a burst path for initial migration so you don't hit soft limits. We'll surface per-key QPS quotas in the console.

Migration pattern
1) Export current vectors + metadata (IDs, timestamps).
2) Sample 1–2% for evaluative A/B (1536 vs 1024) on your known queries — measure top-k and MRR.
3) If 1024 passes thresholds, run bulk re-embed in staged batches (dual-write: write both old provider outputs and Redwood embeddings into a side index).
4) Run shadow traffic: route queries to Redwood but keep results for comparison; once stable, cutover with small percentage traffic shift and monitor.

Auth & deployment
- Hosted: API keys (rotation via Secrets Manager) + per-key quotas.
- Dedicated/Private: mTLS, VPC peering, and HSM/KMS integrations supported for enterprise. We can provide Terraform modules and onboarding docs for Private installs.

Routing & rerank
- Typical pipeline: ANN candidate retrieval (lightweight model or vector index) -> cross-encoder reranker (structured output/tool-calling or model chain). Use per-request routing policies to prefer cheaper model variants and fallback to higher-quality rerankers on misses.

I'll bring a short migration checklist and an example Python script for batching/ingest to the deep-dive.

—Dev
